final_proof:
Write
\[
I_{x,y}=\int_x^y f(t)\,dt.
\]
We use the tagged-partition characterization of the Riemann integral. If
\(P=(x_0,\ldots,x_n;\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)\) is a tagged partition of \([x,y]\), define
\[
S(f,P)=\sum_{j=1}^n f(\xi_j)(x_j-x_{j-1}),
\qquad
\|P\|=\max_j(x_j-x_{j-1}).
\]
If \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([x,y]\) with integral \(I_{x,y}\), then for every \(\eta>0\) there is \(\delta>0\) such that every tagged partition \(P\) of \([x,y]\) satisfying \(\|P\|<\delta\) also satisfies
\[
|S(f,P)-I_{x,y}|<\eta.
\]
This characterization applies to complex-valued functions as well; equivalently, it follows by applying the real characterization to the real and imaginary parts. Since \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), it and its restrictions to closed subintervals are Riemann integrable.

First suppose \(a<c<b\), and put
\[
A=I_{a,c},\qquad B=I_{c,b},\qquad C=I_{a,b}.
\]
Let \(\varepsilon>0\). Apply the preceding characterization, with error tolerance \(\varepsilon/3\), to the integrals \(A,B,C\). This gives positive numbers \(\delta_1,\delta_2,\delta_3\), respectively. Set
\[
\delta=\min(\delta_1,\delta_2,\delta_3).
\]
Choose tagged partitions \(P_1\) of \([a,c]\) and \(P_2\) of \([c,b]\), each having mesh less than \(\delta\). Such partitions exist, for example by dividing each interval into sufficiently many equal subintervals. Joining them at \(c\) produces a tagged partition \(P\) of \([a,b]\). Moreover,
\[
\|P\|=\max(\|P_1\|,\|P_2\|)<\delta
\]
and, since the subintervals of \(P\) are precisely those of \(P_1\) and \(P_2\),
\[
S(f,P)=S(f,P_1)+S(f,P_2).
\]
Therefore, by the triangle inequality in \(\mathbb C\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|C-(A+B)|
&\le |C-S(f,P)|+|S(f,P_1)-A|+|S(f,P_2)-B|\\
&<\frac{\varepsilon}{3}+\frac{\varepsilon}{3}+\frac{\varepsilon}{3}
=\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because this holds for every \(\varepsilon>0\), we must have \(|C-(A+B)|=0\). Hence \(C=A+B\).

If \(c=a\), then \(\int_a^c f(t)\,dt=\int_a^a f(t)\,dt=0\), so the claimed equality reduces to \(0+I_{a,b}=I_{a,b}\). If \(c=b\), it similarly reduces to \(I_{a,b}+0=I_{a,b}\). Thus, in every case,
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\int_a^c f(t)\,dt+\int_c^b f(t)\,dt
=\int_a^b f(t)\,dt}.
\]
